Jordan to share hosted pricing tiers and Dedicated options (by 2025-12-04)
Brightlane to confirm pilot scope and target traffic (by 2025-12-10)

summary: Quick hosted API walkthrough focused on chat/text generation fundamentals: streaming behaviors, key generation parameters (max_tokens, temperature, top_p), retry/backoff patterns, and how Redwood Optimize suggestions can reduce token cost. Customer is evaluating a pilot for Brightlane's patient messaging product; main concerns were latency, percent of partial streams, idempotency, and regulatory logging.
transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-12-02 15:00 UTC | Duration: ~47 min | Attendees listed above

00:00 Jordan: okay everyone, thanks for joining, this is Jordan from Redwood, i'm joined by Priya, our solutions engineer. quick check, audio okay?
00:07 Camila: yep, loud and clear. thanks for setting this up.
00:12 Jordan: awesome. goal for today is a focused hosted API walkthrough — we'll demo streaming behavior, show how generation params change outputs and costs, and cover retry patterns you can use in client code. we'll end with next steps for a pilot. sound good?
00:26 Camila: yes. Ethan, you good?
00:29 Ethan: good. ready.
00:31 Priya: i'll take the live demo bits, show console traces and a quick Optimize suggestion. Jordan will cover pricing/tiers.
00:40 Jordan: great. quick context — Brightlane mentioned patient messaging where average prompt length is ~150 tokens and responses average 220 tokens; target p95 latency < 600ms and sensitive PHI rules mean you want audit logs and optional VPC. correct?
00:55 Camila: correct. plus we want a retriable client behavior if a request fails with transient 503s — we can't have duplicate messages in some flows.
01:03 Jordan: perfect. we'll hit idempotency and dedup tokens later.
01:08 Priya: ok switching to demo screen— pulling up hosted API console. (screen share)
01:15 Jordan: quick note, the console shows a live request inspector, traces per token, and cost breakdown. you can also toggle streaming on/off.
01:24 Priya: i'm going to run a baseline chat call with streaming enabled, model set to redwood-3b-open (example), max_tokens 256, temperature 0.6. watch the stream — you should see partial deltas appear as SSE events.
01:38 [01:38] Priya: (runs request)
01:40 Priya: there! chunk 1, chunk 2 — you can see the partials arrive within 120-180ms for small tokens. sometimes the first packet is metadata.
01:50 Sam: does streaming always mean lower latency?
01:53 Priya: generally yes for perceived latency because tokens show up incrementally. end-to-end p95 depends on model compute and network. for short replies streaming is big win.
02:03 Ethan: what about websocket vs SSE? we prefer websocket for persistent sessions.
02:07 Priya: Redwood supports streaming over HTTP SSE and WebSocket. WebSocket reduces per-request handshake overhead for persistent chat sessions. SSE is simpler for server-sent events and works well for web clients.
02:18 Camila: any difference in retry semantics?
02:21 Priya: same semantics; you just need client logic to resume or detect partials. we typically recommend using idempotency_key on the request and a small at-least-once retry with dedup on server side if you control backend — or use idempotency token to let Redwood drop duplicates.
02:36 Jordan: also note there's a concept of prefix caching and KV cache — if your bot repeats a lot of scaffolding (greetings, system prompts) caching reduces cost and latency.
02:48 Ethan: hmm ok. show me the SDK example for retries?
02:51 Priya: sure. i'll paste a Node snippet; it's in the demo repo. gist link? (posts link) the recommended pattern is exponential backoff with jitter, max attempts 4, and abort for 4xx errors except 429; treat 429 as retryable with backoff. include in the payload an idempotency_key header to avoid duplicate side effects if a retry succeeds twice.
03:12 Sam: do you have an example of a 2-step request where the first is a create and the second is a generate? we want to avoid duplicate creates.
03:20 Priya: if you do a create on your side, best to make that operation idempotent server-side (e.g., client-generated request ID). for the generate call, Redwood's idempotency token helps dedup the generation itself but not downstream business ops. so we recommend making both sides idempotent at the business layer.
03:36 Camila: what about partial responses arriving and our UI showing 'sent' — we want to only mark message delivered once final token arrives. any guidance?
03:44 Priya: show the stream to the user progressively but mark delivered only after stream end event. if stream is cut off you can retry with the same idempotency key and server will return the same result or a compatible continuation depending on the model variant. there are edge cases with stateful session caches where you may need conversation offset markers.
04:06 Jordan: quick pause — pricing implication: streaming doesn't add extra token cost beyond the generated tokens, but longer-lived connections mean more billing for simultaneous open connections in Dedicated scenarios; hosted is usage/tokens-first.
04:20 Camila: good to know. okay continue.
04:24 Priya: switching to parameters. common knobs: max_tokens, temperature, top_p, frequency_penalty, presence_penalty, stop sequences, and logit_bias. small temperature changes can move from deterministic to creative. top_p does nucleus sampling — for clinical safety we often keep temperature 0 - 0.3 and top_p at 0.9 or 1.0.
04:48 Ethan: do you have defaults?
04:50 Priya: default in console runs at temp 0.7 for general demo models, but for Brightlane we'd recommend a conservative default 0.2. you can set per-route defaults in the Console so teams don't accidentally spin up creative outputs.
05:04 Sam: any guardrails for PII?
05:07 Priya: Redwood has redaction integrations and customer-managed prompt sanitizers are recommended before sending. we also support audit logs and optional local logging retention policies when on Private.
05:18 Camila: can we enforce that certain endpoints always use lower temp?
05:21 Priya: yes — route-level configs and policy controls in the Console let you lock params per API key.
05:28 Jordan: let's demo a degraded network case and show retries. Priya?
05:31 Priya: simulating a transient 503 now — (runs test) — client receives 503 at ~06:02 marker, SDK retries with exponential backoff 400ms, 800ms, 1.6s and then success on attempt 3. you can see in the trace the request id and retry count in the inspector.
06:12 Ethan: do retries re-run the generation and could that produce a different response?
06:16 Priya: yes, if you re-issue the same generation without idempotency you may get a different sample. that's why we recommend idempotency_key in the request headers. Redwood will return cached result for identical idempotency key if the original succeeded; if original timed out mid-stream the behavior depends on whether the server committed the output — using idempotency reduces duplicates.
06:38 Camila: how long do you keep idempotency mappings?
06:41 Jordan: by default mapping TTL is 24 hours for hosted; Dedicated can configure retention. we can increase for the pilot if you need longer.
06:50 Sam: curious about partial commits — like if a stream partially delivered and client gives up, what's best practice to resume?
06:58 Priya: two choices: 1) attempt to continue by sending the last N tokens as context and use the same conversation id; 2) retry with idempotency key to get the same full output back, then reconcile with UI. Both have tradeoffs. We typically prefer retry + dedup for transactional flows.
07:20 Camila: ok. show me Optimize suggestions?
07:23 Priya: switching tab — Optimize. here it runs cost vs quality analysis across sample prompts you upload. you can see recommendations — e.g., reduce max_tokens by 15% with minimal quality delta, or suggest a quantized model variant for lower cost. it also flags prompts with high context overhead where prefix caching would help.
07:43 Ethan: is that automatic?
07:44 Priya: it's semi-automated — you upload evaluation prompts and set quality thresholds, then Optimize produces candidate configs and expected token/milli-second savings.
07:55 Jordan: We'll attach a sample Optimize report for your prompt set as part of the follow-up.
07:59 Camila: nice. question — are there region restrictions for PHI? we want logs to stay in us-east-1.
08:06 Jordan: yes hosted supports region pinning for data residency; for stricter compliance we recommend Private deployment or Dedicated in your VPC and KMS.
08:14 Jaya: on the network side, we plan to use VPC egress with strict firewall rules; does Redwood support private endpoints?
08:19 Jordan: yes, Private includes customer-managed networking and on-prem options. Dedicated can integrate with your transit gateway to keep traffic internal.
08:27 Ethan: switching back to retries — what about idempotent tokens collision risk? our clients might accidentally reuse ids.
08:33 Priya: collisions are low if you use UUIDv4 or client-generated ULIDs. we also recommend including a service prefix. on collisions Redwood will return the mapped result for that id.
08:43 Sam: are you able to show raw event frames from streaming? sometimes our engineers want to parse partial JSON chunks.
08:49 Priya: yes — sample SSE frames show event: delta
data: {"token":"Hello","index":1}

09:00 Priya: sometimes transcription in logs shows K-V cache as K-V cash, so apologies if that appears in auto transcriptions, but it's KV cache.
09:09 Camila: (laughs) noted.
09:12 Jordan: moving to error taxonomy briefly — 4xx are client errors, 5xx are transient server errors. 429 is rate limit; recommended handling: backoff and respect Retry-After header. for long-running bursts, consider Dedicated or rate-limiting at your gateway.
09:34 Ethan: do you provide jitter algorithm example?
09:37 Priya: yes — exponential backoff with full jitter (random between 0 and base*2^attempt). we include snippets in the SDKs.
09:45 Camila: can we talk about streaming resume — is there a sequence_number or offset?
09:49 Priya: we include incremental sequence numbers in event frames. you can ack sequence numbers in your client to support resuming. note: resume requires session affinity; if your request routes to a different host and the session wasn't persisted you'll need to replay with idempotency.
10:10 Jordan: i'm going to highlight one more cost tradeoff — lowering temperature or constraining max_tokens is the single biggest lever to cut token spending without a model swap. prefix caching reduces repeated prompt tokens. batching multiple short user messages into a single request can reduce header overhead but may increase latency for interactive sessions.
10:34 Camila: good. Sam: any other security concerns?
10:37 Sam: specifically SSO and RBAC for Console?
10:39 Priya: Console supports SAML SSO, SCIM provisioning, role-based access, and audit logs. for Private deployments you can integrate with your corporate KMS and HSM.
10:50 Camila: ok, this looks reasonable.
10:54 Jordan: quick live failover test — i'm going to switch the route to fallback to a smaller model variant for degraded performance to demonstrate graceful degradation.
11:03 Priya: toggling policy — route fallback set to redwood-quant-2b; new request shows slightly slower but still returns. console shows failover event.
11:15 Ethan: do you do automatic A/B rollouts?
11:18 Priya: yes, Console supports canary rollouts and traffic split rules, plus automatic rollback based on latency or error thresholds.
11:27 Camila: excellent.
11:29 Jordan: time check — we have about 30 minutes left for Q&A and deeper technical bits.
11:34 Camila: can you show the Node SDK streaming pattern that supports pause/resume?
11:38 Priya: yes (pastes) — pattern uses WebSocket, keeps a local buffer of incoming deltas with sequence ids, writes to UI on arrival, and on reconnect queries the inspector with the conversation id to fetch last committed state. code sample in repo.
11:55 Ethan: how do you handle model updates where generation semantics change and could cause regressions?
11:59 Priya: Optimize and the eval suite lets you pin model versions by route. we also have regression alerts based on a prompt set so if a new model introduces distributional shift you get notified.
12:12 Sam: do you keep per-token debug traces? we might need them for incident triage.
12:16 Jordan: yes — traces are available; retention depends on plan. Enterprise/Private have longer retention windows.
12:22 Camila: about telemetry, can we restrict what metadata is collected? PHI concerns.
12:27 Jordan: yes — we can configure scrubbers and require pre-processing before sending; for strictest compliance choose Private with no telemetry forwarded to Redwood.
12:35 Ethan: any known edge cases around SSE dropping mid-stream in mobile networks?
12:40 Priya: mobile networks cause more disconnects; WebSockets with keepalive and retry/backoff logic works better. store partial tokens client-side and reconcile on reconnect.
12:51 Camila: okay, last set of questions — does Redwood charge for aborted streams?
12:56 Jordan: charge is based on tokens generated; if generation was aborted mid-way you'll be billed for the generated tokens. prefix tokens in the prompt are billed as input. We can model billing for pilot to give you estimates.
13:10 Sam: for the pilot we want a budget cap and alerting.
13:13 Jordan: we can set per-team budgeting alerts and quota enforcement in Console.
13:18 Priya: i'm going to run one more demo: a retry that uses idempotency key to get identical output after transient failure. watch inspector request-ids and status.
13:28 [13:28] Priya: (runs) — initial attempt gets 504 due to forced backend slowness, client retries with same id_key, server returns previously stored result and inspector shows 'served from idempotency cache'.
13:46 Ethan: interesting — does that mean the first attempt did finish on the server and was committed?
13:50 Priya: in this sim we forced server to write the result but the network layer cut. idempotency maps to the committed result if it exists. if no committed result exists the retry may re-run generation.
14:05 Camila: from a UI perspective we'll wait for final event before marking delivered. good rule.
14:11 Jordan: ok, time for open Qs — Sam: you started earlier on role-based insights?
14:16 Sam: yes, more on audit logs content — can we get full token-level traces for compliance when asked?
14:21 Jordan: token-level traces can be turned on; we recommend sampling in production for cost, but for audits you can enable full trace retention in Private or Enterprise with separate storage.
14:36 Camila: any final blockers you foresee?
14:39 Jordan: technical wise no — the main items are contractual (data residency, log retention) which we can handle. we'll follow up with a security pack and SOC2 artifact.
14:49 Priya: last note — we'll include a short playbook for retries and idempotency in the follow-up zip.
14:56 Jordan: cool. quick recap of next steps and owners. then we'll close.
15:02 Camila: thanks everyone.
15:05 Jordan: thanks all.

Action items listed in transcript: Priya to send demo repo + SDK snippets; Jordan to attach pricing and enterprise docs; Brightlane to confirm pilot scope and token budget.

End of transcript.
